Are you looking for new opportunities in global development? Check out the latest edition of Devex Jobs Alert, your weekly guide to the most active employers and expert career advice from the world’s largest development job board.

In this week’s issue:

🌍 What finance professionals can expect to earn in development. Mid-level professionals account for the largest share of opportunities, while pay varies considerably by seniority, location, and contract type. Executive positions command the highest salaries, with some consulting assignments also paying particularly well. Major development institutions account for a significant share of recruitment, with finance expertise needed across financial management, financial inclusion and markets, and development finance and investment. Hiring has remained steady into 2026, although average advertised salaries are slightly lower than last year.

💼 What development leaders need from AI. Development leaders do not need to become AI experts, but they increasingly need to understand where the technology can add value, where its limits lie, and how to guide its use across their organizations. Responsible adoption also requires stronger governance around data and AI tools, alongside a willingness to rethink existing workflows rather than simply adding AI to them. Experimentation and change management can help teams identify useful applications and build wider adoption, with leaders playing a central role in steering that process.

California just wrote product requirements for every AI tool used on employees.

Governor Newsom signed a package of workplace AI laws on September 30. What they do, per AP and KQED:

- Bar employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone
- Require written notice to workers when AI causes a mass layoff, relocation or termination (SB 951)
- Ban using biometric data to predict a worker's emotional state, and restrict surveillance tools that infer emotions or collect neural data (AB 1883)
- Ban workplace surveillance tools in bathrooms (AB 1331)
- Direct the state to study AI's effect on hiring and the workforce

What this means if you build or buy workforce AI (my read, not legal advice):

- Firing and discipline features need a **human decision step**
- Emotion-detection features are now a liability in California
- Buyers will push these rules into vendor contracts, so products sold to California employers will be asked to prove compliance

Not every law passed. Newsom also vetoed a bill on AI-generated performer disclosure and one on AI replacing CSU faculty.

If you build or buy workforce AI, which feature would you have to change first?

Meet Arc Studio: Your All-in-One Agent for Building on Arc 🚀

I'll be honest: building onchain used to feel like a club for people who already knew Solidity. You had to set up wallets, gas, contracts, integrations and testnets before you even saw something working. That's a lot for a beginner.

Arc Studio is Circle's answer to that.

It's an AI coding agent that takes plain-language prompts and generates frontend, backend logic and smart contracts for you. You can use it directly in your browser, and it can produce a full-stack app within minutes from a description of the service you want.

What makes it different from a regular AI coding assistant?

It's built specifically around Circle's blockchain infrastructure rather than being a general-purpose tool. That means it already understands the setup that Arc apps run on, so you spend less time fighting configuration.

Features that stood out to me:

🔹 Idea to deployment in one place: Circle describes it as an AI workspace covering the idea, the smart contract logic and the deployment, without turning the process into a black box.

🔹 Multi-chain testing: You can test outputs across nine chains, including Arc, Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche, Polygon and Monad.

🔹 Built for USDC apps: Studio focuses on things like payments, swaps, wallets, bridges, lending, staking and programmable payouts.

🔹 Stablecoin gas: Arc pays fees in USDC instead of a volatile token, so the apps you build can have predictable costs. That ties back to the "gas token barrier" we just covered in the Arc 101 lessons.

Why it's useful:

Beginners: Go from idea to working prototype without years of smart contract experience.

Experienced devs: Move faster and skip repetitive setup.

Founders: Test a payments or finance idea before hiring a full dev team.

It could also make blockchain development accessible beyond specialist smart-contract engineers.

My take: AI tools can still make mistakes, so always review generated contracts before putting real money behind them. But as a way to learn by building, this is one of the friendliest on-ramps to Web3 I've seen.

Would you try building something with Arc Studio? 

Get started 👇
https://studio.arc.io/
